job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 (as amended Oct. 6, 2026): Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, so an operator could split recovery across several vessels, each staying under the cap, with no limit on total output. Nothing aggregates tonnage by operator, affiliate, or project.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "metric tons."** The bill doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry. Freshly recovered nodules carry substantial water, so the choice of measure shifts the effective threshold considerably and invites disputes over compliance.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** "Year" is undefined (calendar, fiscal, or rolling 12 months). An operator could also arguably reset the count by transferring a vessel between affiliates mid-year.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "more than 10,000."** The threshold is exclusive, so exactly 10,000 tons per vessel is lawful. This is minor but reinforces the per-vessel gap.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery."** The term is undefined. It's unclear whether recovery occurs when a seafloor collector picks up nodules, when material is lifted through a riser, or when it is landed on deck. A collector vehicle or riser system may not itself be a "vessel," and material could arguably be stockpiled on the seabed or transferred at sea.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "depths greater than 200 meters."** The bill doesn't specify water depth below the surface versus depth beneath the seabed floor. "From the seabed" also leaves sub-seafloor extraction (e.g., borehole or drilling methods) open to argument.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources."** The term is undefined. It could sweep in sand, gravel, or phosphorite, or arguably exclude seafloor massive sulfides and cobalt-rich crusts depending on interpretation. That breadth or narrowness invites litigation.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary."** "Secretary" is never defined. The bill doesn't say whether it means Commerce (NOAA administers the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act), Interior (BOEM handles OCS minerals), or another official. This makes (B) arguably inoperative until clarified.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B), open-ended delegation.** Letting an official designate "any activity" as prohibited, with no procedure, standards, or rulemaking requirement, invites nondelegation and due-process challenges. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches up to 10 years' imprisonment, a vagueness challenge is especially strong. After *Loper Bright* (2024), agency interpretations of "comparable risks" would also get no deference.

10. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person," corporations.** Only corporations "organized under the laws of a State" are covered. Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies fall outside, so mining abroad through an offshore affiliate appears lawful. LLCs, partnerships, and trusts may not qualify as "corporations," and "State" is undefined, so D.C. and territorial entities may be excluded.

11. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person," individuals.** The definition covers citizens but not lawful permanent residents.

12. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The definition is used only in the Sec. 4 registry, not in the prohibition itself, which refers just to "vessel." Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less escape registration entirely. "Equipped for" lets operators avoid coverage by removing or modularizing recovery gear between voyages.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

13. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** The geographic scope is undefined. It's unclear whether it reaches the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone or the continental shelf. If not, a foreign company operating a foreign-flagged vessel in the U.S. EEZ may not be covered at all.

14. **Sec. 3(a), U.S.-flagged vessels.** The prohibition doesn't reach U.S.-flagged vessels operated by non-U.S. persons on the high seas. It also doesn't reach any vessel "subject to the jurisdiction of the United States."

15. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in."** Financing, chartering, insuring, processing, purchasing, and importing seabed minerals are not addressed. With no import ban, nodules recovered by foreign entities can still enter the U.S. market. Aiding-and-abetting liability would exist for criminal charges via 18 U.S.C. § 2, but there is no secondary liability for civil penalties.

16. **Sec. 3(a), "person."** "Person" is undefined. It's unclear whether federal, state, or foreign government entities or state-owned enterprises are covered.

17. **Sec. 3(b), scope of the exemption.** This is the largest loophole. It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license" without limiting the activity to exploration. This arguably grandfathers full commercial-scale recovery by any pre-enactment license holder, with no tonnage cap and no end date.

18. **Sec. 3(b), which licenses.** The bill doesn't say who must issue the license. It could mean NOAA under DSHMRA, an ISA exploration contract, or any foreign sponsoring state's license, which would let operators qualify through foreign licensing.

19. **Sec. 3(b), renewals and transfers.** It's unclear whether renewals, extensions, amendments, or transfers of pre-enactment licenses keep the exemption. A license could potentially be sold or extended indefinitely.

20. **Sec. 3(b), commercial recovery permits.** Holders of existing DSHMRA *commercial recovery* permits get no grandfathering, while mere exploration licensees arguably do. That is an irrational distinction a court could scrutinize. Permit holders may also assert takings or reliance claims, though courts often hold permits are not property, so this is a litigation risk rather than a sure win.

21. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment" exemption.** The term is undefined, with no permit requirement, tonnage cap, oversight, or rule against selling recovered material. Because it turns on subjective "purpose," commercial recovery could be relabeled as assessment, much like "scientific" whaling. It's also unclear who decides whether the purpose is genuine.

## Sec. 4: Registry

22. **Sec. 4, no penalty for noncompliance.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register or report carries no penalty under this Act. False certifications might reach 18 U.S.C. § 1001, but nothing here says so.

23. **Sec. 4(b), report content.** Reports need only "describe recovery activities." Tonnage, location, depth, and material type aren't required, so the reports can't verify compliance with the Sec. 2(1)(A) threshold. They are also self-certified, with no verification.

24. **Sec. 4, missing enforcement tools.** There is no deadline to register and "operator" is undefined. The bill provides no inspection, observer, boarding, vessel-monitoring, recordkeeping, or subpoena authority.

25. **Sec. 4, geographic scope.** It's unclear whether foreign-flagged covered vessels operating abroad must register. If so, the bill raises international-law and enforceability issues it doesn't address.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

26. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcing agency.** No agency is authorized to assess penalties, investigate, or bring suit, and no procedure or venue is specified. If an agency assesses penalties administratively, *SEC v. Jarkesy* (2024) supports a Seventh Amendment jury-trial challenge.

27. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing conflict.** Sec. 5(a) penalizes violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 makes the Act effective 180 days later. This internal inconsistency gives defendants an argument, and conduct in the 180-day window arguably can't violate a not-yet-effective prohibition.

28. **Sec. 5(a), per-day penalty vs. annual threshold.** The violation is defined by annual tonnage, but the penalty runs "for each day." The bill doesn't say whether a violation begins on the day the 10,000th ton is exceeded, covers every day of recovery that year, or arises only at year-end. That makes penalty calculation contestable.

29. **Sec. 5, no forfeiture.** There is no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or recovered minerals, and no injunctive-relief authority. Fines may simply become a cost of doing business for a well-capitalized operator.

30. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** This standard generally requires proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful. Combined with the definitional ambiguities above, that makes criminal convictions hard to obtain.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

31. **Sec. 6, deadline ambiguity.** It's unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to *beginning* negotiations or *concluding* them. Either way, "shall seek to negotiate" is hortatory, with no reporting requirement or consequence.

32. **Sec. 6, separation of powers.** Directing the Executive's diplomatic negotiations raises foreign-affairs concerns under *Zivotofsky v. Kerry* (2015). The section also doesn't address the ISA/UNCLOS framework or DSHMRA's existing reciprocating-state provisions.

## Sec. 7: Duration

33. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), internal conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition continues until Congress acts by joint resolution, while (b) ends the whole Act at 10 years regardless. The bill doesn't say which controls if no resolution passes, or whether (a) could end the ban earlier.

34. **Sec. 7(a), the National Academies report.** Nothing directs or funds the National Academies to produce the report the trigger depends on. "Serious harm" is undefined. And because a joint resolution requires presentment, it is just a new law, so (a) adds nothing legally.

35. **Sec. 7(b), sunset date.** The sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date, so the ban operates for only about 9.5 years. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) likely preserves penalties for violations before the sunset, but the bill has no express savings clause.

## Sec. 8 and Structural Gaps

36. **Sec. 8, transition window.** The 180-day delay leaves a window for unrestricted operations. Licenses issued during the window aren't grandfathered under Sec. 3(b), since that provision is keyed to enactment, but activity during the window is unregulated.

37. **Relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or reconcile DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.) or OCSLA hard-mineral leasing. That leaves conflicting statutory schemes and pending applications in legal limbo.

38. **No rulemaking authority, appropriations, or severability clause.** Courts generally presume severability, but if Sec. 2(1)(B) is struck down, litigants will argue about what survives.

---

**A strategic note for markup:** Most of these are fixable drafting errors. Raising them publicly at markup could prompt the bill's supporters to correct them in a revised amendment, which would strengthen the bill. You may want to distinguish:

- **Likely to be fixed if raised:** the undefined "Secretary," the Sec. 5/Sec. 8 timing conflict, the Sec. 7 conflict, and the missing enforcement authority.
- **Durable litigation or policy arguments:** the vagueness of Sec. 2(1)(B) paired with criminal penalties, *Jarkesy* jury-trial issues, the treatment of existing permit holders, and extraterritorial reach.

I'm happy to sort the list that way, or to draft talking points or questions for committee members.
